INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
Professor Francesco Parisi is the Oppenheimer
Wolff and Donnelly Professor of Law at the University
of Minnesota Law School and a Professor of Economics
at the University of Bologna. His scholarship applies
economic analysis to legal institutions, including jury
size, voting rules, standards of proof, hung juries, and
retrials.1
Professor Parisi has a longstanding interest in jury
design and standards of proof . He has written extensively on the topic , including  Beyond Six Versus
Twelve: Kian v. Florida and the Design of the Criminal
Jury (2026); Juries in Flux  (with Ram Singh,
2026); Accuracy of Verdicts Under Different Jury Sizes
and Voting Rules  (with Alice Guerra and Barbara
Luppi, 2020);  Quantifying Reasonable Doubt  (with
Daniel Pi and Barbara Luppi, 2020); and  Jury Size
and the Hung -Jury Paradox  (with Barbara Luppi,
2013).

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Petitioner’s functional argument is that twelve -
person juries produce superior adjudicatory outcomes,
including that they are uniformly more protective of
criminal defendants. Petitioner and its supporting
amici, however, rel y on empirical scholarship that
does not establish that  proposition. Instead, t heir
cited studies often measure representation or deliberative process. They do  not speak to the ultimate distribution of convictions, acquittals, and mistrials. In

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in
part, and no party, party’s counsel, or person other than amicus
or his counsel made a monetary contribution intended to fund its
preparation or submission.

2
addition, s everal of the studies involve civil juries,
mock juries, or the composition of jury pools. They are
not a controlled comparison of criminal outcomes under otherwise identical six - and twelve -person systems.
These studies do establish that twelve -person juries are more likely to include members of minority
groups. They also show that larger juries often deliberate longer, recall more evidence, and give minority
viewpoints a greater chance to be heard.
These are serious and important institutional benefits that should not be minimized. But they do not
show that larger juries are more protective of defendants. That shortcoming is underscored by the literature on hung juries. Conventional probability reasoning predicts that unanimity becomes more difficult as
jurors are added. Yet the empirical studies survey ed
in the hung-jury literature generally found no significant difference in deadlock rates between six - and
twelve-person juries. Barbara Luppi & Francesco Parisi, Jury Size and the Hung-Jury Paradox, 42 J. Legal
Stud. 399, 402– 05 (2013). Differences among jurors,
deliberative dynamics, and informational cascades
can offset — and in some cases reverse — the effect of
jury size. The functioning of the two sizes of juries may
differ, while the observed rate of unresolved prosecutions remains similar.
More fundamentally, deadlock is neither a conviction nor an acquittal. A mistrial may lead to retrial,
dismissal, or a plea. The best comprehensive study reported that only about 32 percent of hung -jury cases
proceeded to a second jury trial; among the remainder,
many were dismissed or resolved by plea. Paula L.
Hannaford-Agor, et al., Are Hung Juries a Problem?
26-28 (Nat’l Ctr. for State Courts 2002). Court records
frequently replace the initial deadlock with the case’s

3
final disposition, so reliable nationwide data linking
the first jury’s deadlock to the final outcome are
scarce. A functional analysis should not rest on an empirical chain whose most critical  link is largely unobserved.
Economic theory provides a second reason for caution. Condorcet’s jury theorem shows that a larger
group deciding by majority rule is more likely to be
correct when voters are independent and each is more
likely than not to choose correctly. But criminal juries
do not operate under that model after Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83 (2020). Conviction requires unanimity, and most jurisdictions also require unanimity
for acquittal. Under two -sided unanimity, adding jurors decreases the probability of both unanimous convictions and unanimous acquittals and increases the
residual probability of a deadlock.
That tradeoff does not affect all defendants alike.
A factually guilty 2  defendant may benefit when a
larger jury makes conviction more difficult and shifts
cases toward mistrial. A factually innocent defendant,
however, has an interest not merely in avoiding conviction but in receiving a prompt, definitive acquittal.
For that defendant, a larger jury can reduce the likelihood of correct acquittal by more than it reduces the
likelihood of a wrongful conviction. The resulting
deadlock permits a potential retrial at the State’s discretion. In most situations , this prevents factually

2 For clarity, this brief uses “factually guilty” and “factually innocent” to indicate whether a defendant committed the
charged act, while reserving “legal guilt” for guilt established under the prosecution’s burden of proof. See Tamara Rice Lave, et
al., Juries on Trial 4–5, in LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CRIME AND
PUNISHMENT (Klaus Mathis & Avishalom Tor eds., Springer Nature forthcoming 2027).

4
innocent defendants from obtaining the vindication
and finality of an acquittal.
Increasing jury size is therefore a double -edged
sword in terms of protecting defendants . It may reduce the risk of conviction, including wrongful conviction, but it may also shift cases from potential acquittal to mistrial, denying factually innocent defendants
the prompt vindication and finality afforded by a “not
guilty” verdict. A complete analysis must account for
the cost of these unresolved prosecutions, retrial
rates, the effective standard of proof, and the selection
of cases that reach trial. Once those variables are included, no general economic argument establishes
that twelve-person juries are functionally superior to
six-person juries. The Constitution therefore should
not be reinterpreted on the premise that such a consensus exists.
Accordingly, the judgment should be affirmed. If
the Court nevertheless holds that the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments require twelve jurors, it should
make clear that neither its decision  in this case  nor
Ramos reaches the question of whether  a State  has
the authority to permit acquittal by a substantial nonunanimous majority. This clarification would preserve
State authority to mitigate the burden jury enlargement may place on innocent defendants without
weakening Ramos’s unanimity safeguard against conviction.

5

ARGUMENT
I. The Empirical Record Identifies Benefits of
Larger Juries But Does Not Establish Superior Outcomes.
Williams v. Florida asked whether six jurors could
perform the essential functions of the criminal jury.
399 U.S. 78, 99– 103 (1970). Petitioner answers that
question by invoking research developed after Williams, much of it anticipated in Ballew v. Georgia, 435
U.S. 223, 231–39 (1978). That literature demonstrates
meaningful differences between six - and twelve-person groups. But identifying a difference is not the
same as establishing a constitutionally relevant inferiority. The proper unit of functional analysis is the
jury system, not jury size in isolation. See Francesco
Parisi, Beyond Six Versus Twelve: Kian v. Florida and
the Design of the Criminal Jury , Pub. Choice §§ 2 –4
(2026).3
A.  Petitioner Correctly Identifies Important
Benefits of Larger Juries.
The case for larger juries begins with representation. A larger random sample is more likely to contain
members of groups that comprise a minority of the eligible population. That point is mathematical and important. It also finds empirical support. In a s tudy of
277 civil trials in Cook County, Illinois, approximately
28 percent of six-person juries had no Black member,
compared with about 2 percent of twelve -person juries, and approximately 66 percent of six-person juries
had no Hispanic member, compared with about 40

3 Available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11127-026-01464-
9.

6
percent of twelve-person juries. Shari S. Diamond , et
al., Achieving Diversity on the Jury: Jury Size and the
Peremptory Challenge, 6 J. Empirical Legal Stud. 425,
434–35, 443–49 (2009).
Diversity can improve deliberation. An experiment
involving jury -eligible adults found that racially diverse mock juries considered a wider range of information, discussed more facts, made fewer factual errors, and were more willing to address race-related issues than all -white juries. Samuel R. Sommers, On
Racial Diversity and Group Decision Making , 90 J.
Personality & Soc. Psych. 597, 606-08 (2006). A metaanalysis likewise reported that larger juries generally
deliberated longer and, in one study of mock criminal
juries, discussed trial testimony more accurately. Michael J. Saks & Mollie Weighner Marti, A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Jury Size , 21 L . & Hum. Behav.
451, 457–61 (1997).
Composition may also affect outcomes. A study of
felony trials in two Florida counties found a substantial racial gap in conviction rates when the jury pool
was all white, but no statistically significant gap when
the pool included at least one Black prospective juror.
Shamena Anwar, Patrick Bayer & Randi Hjalmarsson, The Impact of Jury Race in Criminal Trials, 127
Q.J. Econ. 1017, 1034 –35, 1049 (2012). That finding
properly highlights how the source pool, voir dire, and
jury composition shape adjudication.
This Court has long recognized the jury’s role in
guarding against governmental overreach and bringing community judgment into the courtroom. See, e.g.,
Duncan v. Louisiana, 391 U.S. 145, 156 (1968). More
representative juries can advance those values. These
studies thus merit consideration. They show that jury
size can affect representation and deliberative process. They also explain why twelve-person juries may

7
be desirable as a matter of policy even if the Constitution permits six.
The limits of these studies, though, are equally important. The Diamond study involved civil juries in
just one county. The Sommers study involved mock juries and isolated racial composition , rather than jury
size. The Anwar study concerns the racial composition
of the venire and resulting seated jury, not a controlled six -versus-twelve comparison. The Saks and
Marti meta-analysis synthesized heterogeneous studies, many experimental or civil. These limitations do
not negate the findings. But they do mean that process
measures cannot simply be relabeled as proof that one
jury size produces superior criminal outcomes across
jurisdictions.
If the empirical concern is demographic exclusion,
a rule constitutionalizing jury size is an indirect intervention that leaves the direct determinants of the
jury-pool problem unresolved. The existence of alternative and complementary tools , such as reforming
source lists, summons practices, hardship excusals,
voir dire, and peremptory challenges, further weakens
any claim of functional superiority or constitutional
necessity based on representation alone.
B.  The Hung-Jury Literature Undermines
Any Simple Claim of Functional Superiority.
The rule of jury unanimity further complicates the
evidence on the relative performance of differently
sized juries. A twelve -person jury may contain more
information and more viewpoints, but more jurors also
create more potential points of disagreement. Under a
simple model in which jurors vote independently and
each possible vote has positive probability, the probability of unanimous agreement falls as the number of

8
jurors rises. That prediction supports the common
claim that larger juries will hang more often.
The observed evidence has not cleanly confirmed
that prediction , however . The studies surveyed by
Luppi and Parisi generally found no statistically significant difference in hung-jury rates between six- and
twelve-person juries. See Luppi & Parisi, supra, at
402–05. That is the hung-jury paradox: the theoretical
predictions and the observed outcomes diverge.
But the paradox is not evidence that jury size has
no effect. It is instead evidence that the effect is mediated by behavior. Jurors differ in competence, confidence, evidentiary thresholds, and willingness to
maintain dissent. Deliberation can produce informational cascades , and  a lone dissenter may be more
likely to revise a view when faced with a larger apparent consensus. The additional perspectives supplied
by a larger jury can generate disagreement, while the
social influence of a larger majority can reduce it.
Those forces can offset one another, leaving similar
observed deadlock rates even though the deliberative
processes differ. Id. at 405–16.
This matters for Petitioner’s claim that smaller juries disproportionately harm defendants by reaching
fewer deadlocks. See Pet. Br. 31 –34. That assertion
may be a plausible prediction, but it is not a settled
empirical fact. Ballew  itself reviewed evidence suggesting that smaller juries might hang less often. See
435 U.S. at 236. The later literature does not yield a
stable, contemporary national estimate establishing
the magnitude or even the persistence of that relationship between six and twelve.
The studies are also dated. The most comprehensive court -based hung -jury project examined cases
from 1996 through 1998. Hannaford -Agor, et al., supra, at 26–28. Changes in charging, plea bargaining,

9
jury selection, trial length, digital evidence, and prosecutorial practice may affect both deadlock and its aftermath. It would be a mistake to fault Williams for
relying on sparse 1970 evidence and treat that limited
body of older evidence as conclusive of the national experience in 2026 , let alone the basis for a n enduring
constitutional rule.
Larger juries may have representational and deliberative advantages and deliberate differently from
smaller juries. But the empirical record does not establish that twelve-person juries produce more deadlocks, fewer deadlocks, or more defendant -protective
outcomes. On one of the central pathways through
which size is said to affect defendants, the jury is still
out.
C.  The Available Evidence Does Not Link
Jury Size to Final Outcomes.
Even a reliable estimate of first -trial deadlock
would not answer the question  of the superior jury
size. A hung jury is an intermediate event. It may be
followed by a second jury trial, a guilty plea, dismissal,
or prosecutorial abandonment. A verdict measure
asks what the first jury did. An outcome measure asks
what ultimately happened to the defendant. Th e two
are not interchangeable. Parisi, Beyond Six Versus
Twelve, supra, §§ 3–4; Francesco Parisi & Ram Singh,
Juries in Flux, 206 Pub. Choice 391, 411–17 (2026).
The legal distinction is clear. A jury ’s inability to
agree does not terminate the process, and retrial after
a hung jury ordinarily does not violate the Double
Jeopardy Clause. Richardson v. United States, 468
U.S. 317, 323 –26 (1984); Arizona v. Washington , 434
U.S. 497, 505 (1978). A mistrial therefore cannot be
counted as an acquittal merely because it prevents immediate conviction.

10
The data needed to trace that intermediate event
to a final disposition are unusually poor. Court information systems often record the later plea, dismissal,
or retrial outcome in place of the initial deadlock because a hung jury is not a final disposition. In its
study, the National Center for State Courts  reported
that approximately 32 percent of hung-jury cases proceeded to a second jury trial , 21.6 percent were dismissed, and 31.8 percent produced a guilty plea. Hannaford-Agor, et al., supra, at 26– 28; Parisi & Singh,
supra, at 411 –13 & nn.35 –39. Of the cases that
reached a second jury, 69 percent resulted in conviction, 19 percent in acquittal, 8 percent in another
hung jury, and 4 percent in another form of mistrial.
Hannaford-Agor, et al., supra, at 28. Those figures are
informative but neither current nor nationally representative.
The absence of data connecting initial jury size to
ultimate outcomes  precludes confident claims about
outcome accuracy.  A larger jury might improve the
conditional reliability of verdicts when a verdict is
reached yet leave more cases unresolved. A smaller
jury might reach more verdicts, or reach them through
a different deliberative path, while producing a similar final distribution after prosecutorial selection and
plea bargaining. If deadlocked cases are frequently
dismissed, deadlock resembles non -conviction for a
factually guilty defendant but still lacks the formal finality of acquittal for a factually innocent defendant .
If deadlocked cases are routinely retried, the first
jury’s decisiveness matters less, but the defendant
bears the cost and risk of another trial.
Selection before trial compounds the problem.
Prosecutors choose which charges to file and which
weak cases to dismiss; defendants choose whether to
plead; judges rule on evidence; and both sides shape

11
the seated jury. A change in jury size can alter plea
incentives and the mix of cases that reach trial. Observed conviction rates are therefore endogenous to
institutional design. A jurisdiction with a lower trial
conviction rate therefore may not have less accurate
juries; it may try a different pool of cases. See Parisi,
Beyond Six Versus Twelve, supra, § 3.
There is accordingly no empirical basis for the categorical claim that twelve-person juries produce superior outcomes  in criminal cases . The evidence supports a more nuanced proposition: jury size affects
several important features of adjudication, sometimes
in opposing directions, and those effects are filtered
through voting rules, retrials, standards of proof, and
case selection. That proposition counsels against overruling Williams based on evidence that is ultimately
inconclusive on the central question of superiority.
II. Where Unanimity is Required, A Larger
Jury Is a Double-Edged Sword for Defendants.
A. Condorcet’s Jury Theorem Does Not Resolve the Choice Between Six and Twelve
Under Unanimity.
The strongest theoretical intuition favoring larger
groups comes from Condorcet. If voters decide by majority rule, vote independently, and are each  more
likely than not to choose the correct alternative, adding voters increases the probability that the majority
is correct. Marquis de Condorcet, Essai Sur L’Application De L’Analyse À La Probabilité Des Décisions Rendues À La Pluralité Des  Voix (1785). The insight is
powerful: independent information aggregates, and
individual errors tend to cancel.

12
But the theorem ’s institutional assumptions matter. A majority-vote rule always produces an outcome,
except for a possible tie that can be resolved by an odd
group size or a tie -breaking rule. A unanimous jury
can produce another result: no verdict. Adding jurors
can improve the information in the room while making the required agreement more difficult. The model
must therefore distinguish the correctness of verdicts
from the decisiveness of the process.
Strategic and correlated voting further complicate
the classical theorem. Jurors deliberate rather than
cast isolated ballots. Their votes may respond to common evidence and shared biases. See Timothy J.
Feddersen & Wolfgang Pesendorfer, Convicting the
Innocent: The Inferiority of Unanimous Jury Verdicts
Under Strategic Voting , 92 Am. Pol. Sci. Rev. 23
(1998); Peter J. Coughlan, In Defense of Unanimous
Jury Verdicts, 94 Am. Pol. Sci. Rev. 375 (2000). Th is
literature does not deny the informational advantages
of a larger jury, as articulated above. But it shows why
those advantages cannot provide a solid basis for
claims that larger juries produce superior outcomes.
A further strand in the  economics literature cautions against assuming that  larger juries bring more
to the table . The familiar Condorcet intuition treats
individual jurors’ information and resulting voting as
independent of group size . But if acquiring and processing information requires effort, that assumption
may fail. Mukhopadhaya models juror attention as endogenous and shows that, as the jury size grows, each
juror may have less incentive to invest in acquiring
information and be more likely to free -ride on the effort of fellow jurors. The free-riding effect can offset—
and under some assumptions reverse —the informational advantage commonly attributed to a larger
jury. See Kaushik Mukhopadhaya, Jury Size and the

13
Free Rider Problem, 19 J.L. Econ. & Org. 24, 24, 38 –
40 (2003). Bag, Levine, and Spencer qualify Mukhopadhaya’s strongest result: under alternative equilibria, accuracy may reach a maximum at a particular
jury size and not improve as additional jurors are
added. See Parimal Bag, Paul Levine & Christopher
Spencer, A Note on: Jury Size and the Free Rider Problem, 4 Econ. Bull. 1, 1–2 (2006).
Related research on group deliberation identifies
another possible countervailing effect. A mock -jury
study found that members of large groups did not necessarily contribute equally to collective decisionmaking and that restructuring twelve -person groups into
smaller conversational units increased participants’
perceived equality of contribution and reduced inhibition. See Bridget M. Waller et al., Twelve (Not So) Angry Men: Managing Conversational Group Size Increases Perceived Contribution by Decision Makers, 14
Group Processes & Intergroup  Rel. 835, 835, 839– 40
(2011). Experimental work outside the jury setting
similarly found that discussion in five -person groups
operated more as interactive dialogue, while discussion in ten-person groups tended toward serial monologue in which the dominant sp eaker exercised
greater influence. See Nicolas Fay, Simon Garrod &
Jean Carletta, Group Discussion as Interactive Dialogue or as Serial Monologue: The Influence of Group
Size, 11 Psych. Sci. 481, 481, 483 (2000). These studies
identify another reason to doubt the view that increasing the number of jurors necessarily adds valuable
perspectives.
Finally, there is the risk that larger juries operating under the rule of unanimity may, in addition to
reducing the risk of erroneous verdicts, also reduce
the likelihood of correct verdicts. The mechanism,
again, is deadlock. If one models outcome likeli hood

14
for both factually innocent and factually guilty defendants, the likelihood of unanimity decreases and
the likelihood of deadlock rises as jury size increases.
Put differently, Condorcet’s monotonic result under
majority rule  does not hold  because unanimity converts some potential correct and incorrect verdicts
into unresolved cases. See Alice Guerra, Barbara
Luppi & Francesco Parisi, Accuracy of Verdicts Under
Different Jury Sizes and Voting Rules , 28 Sup. Ct.
Econ. Rev. 221, 227–36 (2020).
B.  Deadlock Must Be Treated as a Distinct
Cost.
Blackstone’s maxim gives wrongful conviction
greater moral and social weight than wrongful acquittal: it is better that ten guilty persons escape than that
one innocent suffer. 4 William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England 352 (1765). Modern economic analysis expresses the same idea as an error -
cost ratio. The ratio identifies how much more heavily
the legal system values one adjudicatory error than
the other. See Daniel Pi, Francesco Parisi & Barbara
Luppi, Quantifying Reasonable Doubt, 72 Rutgers U.
L. Rev. 455, 468–78 (2020).
That familiar ratio provides the relative weight of
two erroneous verdicts : wrongful conviction and
wrongful acquittal. But a unanimous jury system also
produces deadlocks. The cost of a dead lock is not accounted for on either side of Blackstone’s ratio.
A complete Blackstonian analysis should also account for the costs imposed when the accusation remains unresolved. This expanded accounting prevents
the analysis from treating unresolved prosecutions as
costless.
There are six possible first-trial outcomes: each defendant type ( factually innocent or factually guilty )

15
may be convicted, acquitted, or left without a verdict.
Four of these outcomes  generate adjudicatory losses :
wrongful conviction of the factually innocent , wrongful acquittal of the factually guilty , and deadlock for
each defendant type.
These outcomes are costly, not only for the justice
system, but also for individual defendants, who may
suffer from fewer definitive acquittals. And these outcomes may be more likely for larger juries, even if
larger juries also may improve representation and
conditional verdict reliability. Which jury size minimizes social loss depends on variables separate from
jury size and not measured with sufficient consistency
across jurisdictions.
C.  Jury Enlargement Can Protect Factually
Guilty Defendants While Burdening Factually Innocent Defendants.
The phrase “defendant protection” can obscure an
important distributional effect. A factually guilty defendant and a factually innocent defendant share an
interest in avoiding conviction, but they do not value
the other first -trial outcomes in the same way. The
guilty defendant may prefer deadlock to conviction because it creates another opportunity to avoid punishment. By contrast, t he innocent defendant prefers  a
definitive acquittal, not a mistrial.
If both conviction and acquittal require unanimity,
adding jurors makes both wrongful convictions and
correct acquittals less likely. The first effect is desirable; the second is not. Additionally, as the jury grows
in size, these two effects differ in magnitude. With six
jurors, a wrongful conviction already requires six mistaken votes, leaving comparatively little room for additional jurors to reduce that risk. A correct acquittal

16
is more likely, but it, too, can be blocked by a single
dissenting vote.
Expanding the jury therefore creates more deadlocks that prevent correct acquittals than it prevents
wrongful convictions. In other words, most of the additional deadlock comes at the expense of correct acquittals, not from eliminating wrongful convictions.
Parisi & Singh, supra, at 405–10, 414–17. The mirror
image applies to a factually guilty defendant. Enlarging the jury reduces the probability of a correct conviction by more than it reduces the probability of a
wrongful acquittal.
The resulting increase in deadlock therefore
largely benefits guilty defendants because the predominant shift is away from conviction. Thus, the
same rule change can reduce wrongful convictions
while moving even more cases from correct verdicts—
acquittals or convictions—into the limbo of a deadlock.
This comparison is nonlinear. Increasing jury size
reduces the probabilities of both wrongful conviction
and correct acquittal . As the jury grows, however,
wrongful conviction becomes increasingly rare, leaving progressively less risk for each additional juror to
eliminate. Beyond a threshold that depends on juror
accuracy and the relative harms of these outcomes,
the cost of leaving more innocent defendants without
definitive acquittals exceeds the benefit of preventing
additional wrongful convictions.
Once that threshold is crossed, the marginal costs
of jury expansion outweigh its marginal benefits, rendering further enlargement undesirable. Each additional juror supplies another safeguard against
wrongful conviction but also becomes an obstacle to
correct acquittal. The benefit of preventing wrongful
conviction diminishes rapidly because wrongful conviction requires every juror to err. The cost of

17
preventing correct acquittal grows more rapidly. Jury
enlargement may therefore reach a point at which another juror is more likely to prevent a correct acquittal
than to prevent a wrongful conviction, and the cost of
the former exceeds the benefit of the latter , independently of the weight assigned to wrongful conviction and wrongful acquittals (Blackstonian ratios) in
the local jurisdictions.
 This insight has serious implications . A mistrial
may allow the defendant to go home, but it does not
allow the innocent defendant to go home vindicated.
For the innocent defendant, the limbo of an unresolved prosecution carries distinctive legal and human
costs. The prosecution may retry after a hung jury.
Richardson, 468 U.S. at 323–26. Whether to seek a retrial rests with the State. A n unresolved accusation
lacks the exonerating force of a “ not guilty” verdict.
The Court has recognized that a pending accusation
may expose a defendant to public scorn, damage employment, burden associations, and produce prolonged
anxiety and insecurity. Klopfer v. North Carolina, 386
U.S. 213, 221–22 (1967). And although the State may
retry a deadlocked case, defendants have no general
corresponding right to demand that the State either
prosecute anew or accept entry of an acquittal .
See Francesco Parisi, The Right to a Jury Retrial (Minnesota Legal Studies Research Paper,
2026).4
These costs show why deadlock cannot be counted
as uniformly defendant -protective. By making unanimity harder to achieve, it reduces both unanimous
convictions and unanimous acquittals, shifting cases
at both ends toward deadlock. Under the conventional
assumption that factually guilty defendants are more

18
likely to be convicted and factually innocent defendants are more likely to be acquitted, that shift will
tend to benefit the former by preventing otherwise
correct convictions, while harming the latter by preventing otherwise correct and final acquittals.
This tradeoff must be acknowledged in assessing
the relative merits of larger and smaller juries . Jury
enlargement cannot simply be assumed to provide
greater protection to defendants.  And it undermines
the claim, advanced by Petitioner and his amici, that
twelve-person juries are functionally superior.
The pursuit of uniformity in jury size may, in fact,
produce greater variation in jury outcomes. A constitutional requirement of twelve jurors would alter both
the frequency of deadlock and the consequences of retrial. Those effects, however, depend on prosecutorial
screening, the evidentiary strength of the cases reaching trial, and the treatment of cases following deadlock. Unless those features are also uniform, the same
jury-size rule may operate quite differently across jurisdictions. That raises broader questions of federalism and may well counsel  against a nationwide rule .
At a minimum, standardizing one component of the
jury system does not standardize the system as a
whole.
III. Although Not Presented, One-Sided Unanimity Should Not Be Foreclosed.
The constitutionality of one-sided unanimity is not
encompassed by the question presented in Kian , and
the Court need not decide it to resolve this case. Amicus addresses the issue only because a ruling requiring twelve-person juries would sharpen the burden described above for factually innocent defendants. If the
Court reverses the judgment below , it should clearly
note, consistent with the scope of the question

19
presented in this case, that neither its decision in this
case nor Ramos forecloses a State’ s authority to permit acquittal by a substantial nonunanimous majority.
A. Ramos Requires Unanimity for Conviction But Did Not Address Acquittal.
Ramos held that the Sixth Amendment requires a
unanimous verdict to convict a defendant of a serious
offense. 590 U.S. at 90, 93. The case involved a 10- to-
2 conviction, and its defendant-protective holding concerns the agreement necessary before the State may
impose criminal punishment. I mportantly, it did not
decide that the Constitution requires the same agreement to terminate a prosecution in the defendant’s favor.
Most jurisdictions, including Florida, use two -
sided unanimity as a matter of rule or practice. Florida Rule of Criminal Procedure 3.440 provides that no
verdict may be rendered unless all trial jurors concur.
A State’s decision to require unanimity for both conviction and acquittal does not establish that the Constitution requires unanimity in both directions.  The
constitutional concern that no person be convicted
over a juror’s reasonable doubt is not mirrored when
a substantial majority votes to acquit.
Oregon illustrates the distinction after Ramos. Its
law now requires unanimous agreement for a guilty
verdict but allows a not-guilty verdict with the concurrence of at least ten of twelve jurors. Or. Rev. Stat. §
136.450(1)-(2). That asymmetry preserves the unanimity safeguard against conviction while reducing
the number of cases in which a minority favoring guilt
prevents the final acquittal of a factually innocent defendant.

20
Scholars have likewise defended asymmetric rules
on democratic and defendant -protective grounds. See
Ethan J. Leib, Supermajoritarianism and the American Criminal Jury, 33 Hastings Const. L.Q. 141, 141-
42, 184-96 (2006) (arguing for a demanding threshold
to convict and majority rule to acquit). The optimal
number of votes needed to acquit may depend on jury
size, proof standards, and the social cost of deadlock.
The relevant point is that one -sided unanimity may
mitigate the problems associated with larger juries,
allowing more factually innocent defendants to obtain
a “not guilty” verdict, without weakening the unanimity requirement for conviction. See also Barbara Luppi
& Francesco Parisi, Jury Size and the Blackstonian
Tradeoff (Minn. Legal Stud. Rsch. Paper No. 2026-43,
2026); Francesco Parisi, The Unsettled Side of Unanimity: Jury Verdicts After Ramos (Minn. Legal Stud.
Rsch. Paper No. 2026-44, 2026).5
B.  Nonunanimous Acquittals Can Mitigate
the Burden Jury Enlargement Places on
Innocent Defendants.
If this Court requires twelve jurors, the number of
potential dissenters doubles in jurisdictions that currently use six. Under two -sided unanimity, that
change can move cases away from both conviction and
acquittal. Requiring unanimity to convict prevents
the enlargement from increasing the State’s power to
punish. But requiring unanimity to acquit can cause
the enlargement to reduce the innocent defendant ’s
chance of obtaining final exoneration.
A one-sided rule directly addresses that imbalance.
Suppose conviction still requires all twelve jurors,

while acquittal may be returned by ten, nine, or another legislatively selected majority threshold. The
change does not convert a single vote for acquittal into
a conviction, and thus Ramos remains fully operative.
It instead converts a subset of deadlocks in which a
substantial majority favors acquittal into final not -
guilty verdicts. That reduces retrial exposure and the
stigma of unresolved accusation for defendants whom
most jurors believe should be acquitted.
Amicus, however, is not suggesting constitutionalizing or approving a particular acquittal rule. Doing
so would repeat the error of isolating one design variable from the system in which it operates. It is also
beyond the scope of the question presented in this
case. See Sup. Ct. R. 14.1(a); Yee v. City of Escondido,
503 U.S. 519, 535 (1992) (noting the Court “ordinarily
do[es] not consider questions outside those presented
in the petition for certiorari”).
Accordingly, if the Court reverses, it should make
clear it is not reaching the question of unanimity for
acquittal. That limited clarification would preserve
room for States to mitigate the costs of jury enlargement and preserve adequate protection for factually
innocent defendants, avoiding unnecessary future litigation over Ramos’s reach.
